questions.explanation: Cisco DNA Center uses REST APIs and NETCONF/YANG to push intent-based configurations. It abstracts device-level CLI and automates provisioning, assurance, and policy across the fabric.

questions.question: An access port at a campus edge has Root Guard enabled. A new switch is connected to that port and starts advertising a superior BPDU (lower priority than the current root). Without Root Guard, that BPDU would have caused a re-election. With Root Guard, the port enters root-inconsistent state and drops the superior BPDU. Which threat does Root Guard mitigate?
options: An unauthorised switch winning the STP root-bridge election from where it shouldn't

BPDU flooding from the legitimate root bridge — triggers STP recalculation but is not the threat Root Guard blocks; Root Guard specifically prevents a non-root switch from winning the root-bridge election
Duplicate IP addresses causing STP recalculation (no STP relationship)
ARP spoofing on trunk ports (different L2 attack, handled by DAI not Root Guard)
questions.explanation: Root Guard prevents a port from becoming a root port by blocking any superior BPDU received. This ensures the intended switch remains root bridge, protecting against rogue switches claiming root.

questions.question: A switch port is configured with `authentication port-control auto` and an EAP profile pointing at a RADIUS server. Until the supplicant (PC) authenticates successfully, only EAPOL frames pass through the port; user data (DHCP, ARP, IP) is blocked. After successful 802.1X, the port transitions to the authorised state and forwards normal traffic. Which protocol provides this port-based access control?
options: PoE — IEEE 802.3af/at, supplies power to connected devices; it has no access control or port authentication mechanism and does not restrict which devices may use the port
Auto-negotiation — IEEE 802.3 clause 28, negotiates speed/duplex, not authentication on a port
IEEE 802.1X — port-based network access control: EAP over LAN authentication on a port before traffic is allowed
MACsec — 802.1AE encrypts authenticated traffic on a port but does not perform the initial port-based authentication
questions.explanation: 802.1X (port-based NAC) requires devices to authenticate (via EAP/RADIUS) before they can access the network. Unauthenticated devices are placed in a limited or quarantine VLAN.

questions.question: After configuring 'ntp server 10.0.0.1' on a Cisco router, how does an engineer confirm the router has successfully synchronized its clock, and what output field is the definitive indicator?
options: 'ping 10.0.0.1' — a successful ping proves UDP reachability to the NTP server; it does not verify the clock is synchronized and the stratum relationship is established
'show ntp status' — look for 'Clock is synchronized' with a stratum value and the reference IP;.
'show clock detail' — it displays the NTP server IP and last sync timestamp directly
'debug ntp packets' — the only way to definitively confirm NTP synchronization because show commands may show cached state
questions.explanation: 'show ntp status' is the correct command. Key fields: 'Clock is synchronized' (vs 'unsynchronized'), 'stratum X' (the router's own stratum — one more than the server's), 'reference is <IP>' (the NTP server address), and 'offset' (time difference in ms). A synchronized clock shows all these. 'show clock detail' shows time source (NTP vs manual) but not sync status details. A successful ping to the NTP server only confirms Layer 3 reachability, not NTP protocol synchronization. an unsynchronized clock shows 'Clock is unsynchronized'

questions.question: A router has OSPF and EIGRP both advertising routes to 10.0.0.0/8. Which route is installed in the routing table?
options: OSPF — it uses link-state and is more accurate — false; OSPF has an administrative distance of 110, higher than EIGRP's 90; when both protocols advertise the same prefix, EIGRP wins
Both routes are installed using equal-cost load balancing
EIGRP — it has a lower administrative distance (90 vs 110)
The one with the lower metric wins regardless of protocol
questions.explanation: Administrative distance determines which protocol's route is preferred. EIGRP internal AD = 90, OSPF AD = 110. The EIGRP route wins and is installed in the routing table.

questions.question: An 802.1X-enabled access port relays the supplicant's credentials to a RADIUS server via EAP-over-RADIUS. On Access-Accept, RADIUS attribute exchange can carry additional authorisation: which VLAN to put the port in, ACL filter to apply, session timeout, and so on. The switch then enforces those policies. What information class does RADIUS return beyond pass/fail?
options: A DHCP lease for the supplicant — DHCP is a separate process; the RADIUS server returns authorisation attributes such as VLAN assignment, downloadable ACL, and session timeout, not DHCP leases
Only a pass/fail result — RADIUS can return more in attribute-value pairs
Authorisation attributes: VLAN assignment, downloadable ACL, session timeout, reauth period
Wireless session encryption key — that's separate WPA-Enterprise key derivation, not the RADIUS auth payload
questions.explanation: RADIUS can return Access-Accept with attributes like VLAN assignment, ACLs, and session timeout — enabling dynamic policy assignment per user or device, not just a pass/fail. and authorization attributes in addition to authentication

questions.question: An enterprise VoIP deployment uses UDP for voice packets. A network engineer proposes switching to TCP to solve a persistent 3% packet loss problem affecting call quality. Why would this change most likely WORSEN voice quality despite TCP providing reliable delivery?
options: TCP's segment ordering requires all packets to be buffered until gaps are filled, causing the entire audio stream to pause rather than playing already-received packets
TCP's three-way handshake adds 1.5 RTT of latency before the first voice packet flows, making call setup too slow for real-time communication
TCP's congestion window algorithm would reduce throughput below what G.711 or G.729 codecs require for acceptable audio quality
TCP's retransmission mechanism introduces variable and unpredictable delay (jitter).
questions.explanation: VoIP uses UDP because voice is a real-time, loss-tolerant application. With TCP, a lost packet triggers retransmission and the receiver must wait for it before processing later packets (head-of-line blocking). By the time the retransmitted packet arrives (one RTT later), its play time has passed — it is useless. Silence concealment on 3% UDP loss sounds much better than the jitter and delays TCP retransmission would introduce. RTP over UDP with jitter buffers is the correct architecture for voice. By the time a retransmitted voice packet arrives, it is too late to play in the audio stream — the resulting jitter is MORE damaging to voice quality than the original 3% packet loss

questions.question: A network engineer is reviewing the RSTP topology. Switch A has a port that receives the best BPDU from a non-root switch but does not lead toward the root bridge. What port role is assigned to that port?
options: Alternate port — backup path to root, kept in discarding state
Root port — it provides the best path to the root bridge
Backup port — it is a redundant connection on the same segment
Designated port — it forwards traffic toward the root bridge
questions.explanation: In RSTP, an Alternate port receives a superior BPDU from a neighboring switch (not from the root direction) and is placed in Discarding state as a backup path. If the Root port fails, the Alternate port transitions to Root port quickly without a full topology recalculation.

questions.question: A company is bundling four Gigabit Ethernet links between two distribution switches. The switches are from different vendors. Which EtherChannel negotiation protocol should the engineer use?
options: PAgP active mode — it is the most widely supported Cisco protocol
LACP active mode — it is the IEEE 802.3ad open standard supported by all vendors
Static ON mode — it requires no negotiation protocol and can bring links up regardless of which vendors are at each end; however, there is no dynamic verification, risking misconfigurations
PAgP desirable mode — it negotiates automatically with any vendor
questions.explanation: LACP (Link Aggregation Control Protocol, IEEE 802.3ad) is the open standard for EtherChannel negotiation and is supported by all vendors. PAgP is Cisco-proprietary and will not work with non-Cisco equipment. Static ON mode works but provides no negotiation or error detection.

questions.question: A network engineer assigns the IPv6 address 2001:0db8:abcd::1/64 to a router interface. Which address type does this represent?
options: Link-local address — automatically generated and valid only on the local segment
Unique Local Address — used for private internal routing, not routable on the internet
Global Unicast Address — routable on the public IPv6 internet
Anycast address — assigned to multiple interfaces for load sharing
questions.explanation: 2001:db8::/32 is within the Global Unicast Address range (2000::/3). Global Unicast Addresses are publicly routable. Note: 2001:db8::/32 is reserved for documentation; real GUAs are assigned by IANA/RIRs. Link-local begins with FE80::/10 and Unique Local with FC00::/7.

questions.question: DHCP snooping is enabled on a switch. A port connected to an end-user workstation receives a DHCP Offer message. What does the switch do?
options: Forwards the Offer — DHCP snooping only inspects Request messages
Sends a DHCP Decline back to the rogue server on behalf of the client
Forwards the Offer after logging it in the DHCP snooping binding table
Drops the Offer because DHCP Offer messages are only expected on trusted ports
questions.explanation: DHCP snooping classifies ports as trusted or untrusted. DHCP server messages (Offer, Ack) are only expected from trusted ports (uplinks to real servers). An Offer arriving on an untrusted port indicates a rogue DHCP server and is dropped, protecting clients from receiving malicious IP configuration.

questions.question: Two OSPF routers are connected on an Ethernet segment. A DR and BDR are elected. Which OSPF network type is in use, and what is the function of the DR?
options: Point-to-point network type — no DR/BDR election occurs because there is only one direct link segment between two routers, not a shared multi-access broadcast medium
Broadcast network type — the DR forms full adjacency with all routers on the segment, reducing LSA flooding overhead
NBMA network type — the DR manually specifies which neighbors it will exchange routing information with
Point-to-multipoint network type — the DR is optional and elected only when more than four routers are present
questions.explanation: Ethernet links use OSPF broadcast network type by default. A Designated Router (DR) and Backup DR (BDR) are elected. All other routers (DROthers) form full adjacency only with the DR and BDR, not with each other, reducing the number of adjacencies and LSA flooding on multi-access segments.

questions.question: A network engineer needs to block Telnet traffic originating from a specific host at 192.168.10.5 before it enters the network core. Which ACL type and placement best achieves this with minimal impact?
options: Standard ACL placed close to the destination — standard ACLs match only destination IP
Extended ACL placed close to the destination — to allow fine-grained protocol filtering
Standard ACL placed close to the source — to block the host before traffic traverses the network
Extended ACL placed close to the source.
questions.explanation: Extended ACLs can match on source IP, destination IP, protocol, and port — making them ideal to block specific traffic like Telnet (TCP port 23) from a specific host. Placing an extended ACL close to the source prevents unwanted traffic from consuming bandwidth across the network. to filter by source IP and destination port as early as possible

questions.question: A small branch office uses NAT overload (PAT) with a single public IP address. Host A (192.168.1.10) and Host B (192.168.1.20) both establish HTTP sessions to the same web server. How does the router distinguish return traffic for each host?
options: It uses the unique PAT source port to map each return session to the correct inside host
It forwards return traffic to both hosts and lets the hosts discard packets not meant for them
It uses the destination IP in the returning packet to identify each host
It requires each host to use a different destination port when connecting to the same server
questions.explanation: PAT (overloaded NAT) translates multiple inside private addresses to a single public IP by assigning a unique source port to each session in the NAT translation table. Return traffic arrives at the public IP with that unique destination port, allowing the router to match it back to the correct inside local address.

questions.question: An engineer enables a neighbour-discovery protocol on a campus that mixes Cisco, HP, and Juniper switches. The protocol must be the open, IEEE-defined alternative to Cisco's CDP — not proprietary, runs at Layer 2, advertises identity / capability / system-description TLVs. Which statement correctly compares LLDP to CDP?
options: CDP discovers non-Cisco devices natively — false; CDP is Cisco-proprietary and is not interpreted by HP, Juniper, Arista, or other non-Cisco switches
LLDP (IEEE 802.1AB) is vendor-neutral — works across Cisco, HP, Juniper, Arista, etc.
Both LLDP and CDP are Layer-3 IP-multicast protocols — false, both are L2
LLDP is Cisco-proprietary and CDP is the IEEE open standard — reversed
questions.explanation: LLDP (Link Layer Discovery Protocol, IEEE 802.1AB) is the open standard equivalent of CDP. Both operate at Layer 2 using multicast frames to advertise device identity, capabilities, and port information. CDP only works between Cisco devices; LLDP works across all vendors, making it the preferred choice in mixed-vendor environments. while CDP is Cisco-proprietary and works only between Cisco devices

questions.question: A company is deploying a wireless network and wants to use the strongest commercially available encryption with support for Protected Management Frames. Which wireless security standard should they choose?
options: WEP with 128-bit key — the extended key length provides adequate security for enterprise use
WPA2-Enterprise with CCMP — it provides stronger encryption but does not support management frame protection
WPA3 with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) and mandatory PMF.
WPA2-Personal with TKIP — it is backward-compatible and supports all legacy clients
questions.explanation: WPA3 replaces the PSK four-way handshake with SAE (Dragonfly handshake), which provides forward secrecy and resistance to offline dictionary attacks. WPA3 also mandates Protected Management Frames (PMF/802.11w), protecting against deauthentication attacks. WPA2 with CCMP/AES is still strong but does not mandate PMF or offer forward secrecy. providing forward secrecy and stronger handshake protection

questions.question: A network architect is designing a WAN solution for 50 branch offices. The solution must support centralized policy management, automatic encrypted overlays across any transport (MPLS, broadband, LTE), and zero-touch provisioning for new branches. Which technology best meets these requirements?
options: SD-WAN using a centralized controller — orchestrates overlay tunnels connecting branches over any transport; it is a Layer-3 overlay solution, not Layer-2 Metro Ethernet directly linking all branches
Layer 2 Metro Ethernet connecting all branches to a central hub switch
Traditional hub-and-spoke MPLS with static routing at each branch
DMVPN Phase 3 with spoke-to-spoke tunnels and OSPF summarization
questions.explanation: SD-WAN separates the control plane (centralized controller, e.g., Cisco vManage) from the data plane (edge devices). It automatically builds encrypted overlay tunnels across any underlay (MPLS, internet, LTE), supports Zero Touch Provisioning for new branches, and enforces application-aware routing policies centrally. This is far more flexible and scalable than traditional WAN approaches.

questions.question: You must connect a switch port to a printer that does NOT support DTP. Which TWO commands belong on the switch interface to lock it as an access port and stop trunk negotiation?
options: switchport mode trunk — sets the port as a tagged VLAN trunk rather than an access port; a printer port must be in access mode, not trunk mode
switchport mode access
switchport nonegotiate
no switchport
questions.explanation: `switchport mode access` forces the port into access mode (no trunk). `switchport nonegotiate` disables DTP frames so the port never tries to negotiate trunking with the connected device. `switchport mode trunk` would do the opposite, and `no switchport` makes the port a routed L3 interface.

questions.question: Which TWO statements about OSPF and EIGRP administrative distance are TRUE on a Cisco router with default settings?
options: OSPF (110) is preferred over EIGRP internal (90) when both learn the same prefix
EIGRP internal (90) is preferred over OSPF (110) when both learn the same prefix
EIGRP external routes have an AD of 170, higher than OSPF
Static routes have an AD of 1, preferred over both OSPF and EIGRP
questions.explanation: Lower AD wins. EIGRP internal (90) beats OSPF (110), so the EIGRP route installs in the RIB. EIGRP external is 170 — higher (worse) than OSPF 110. Static routes default to AD 1, preferred over any IGP. The first option reverses the comparison.
